The world is planning for a surge in electricity demand. 

How can this be turned into an opportunity for energy security and socio-economic resilience?

Yesterday, UNDP joined the COP31 Türkiye –IEA–UN High-Level Energy Transition Solutions Dialogue at UN Headquarters. The IEA also released new analysis prepared for the COP31 discussions.

Its findings point to the scale of the opportunity. Electricity could cost-effectively meet 33% of global final energy use by 2035, up from 23% today, putting the proposed 35% goal within reach. In a faster electrification scenario, fuel-importing countries could cut their energy import bills by more than US$400 billion by 2035—reducing exposure to volatile fossil-fuel markets and strengthening energy security.

Accelerating electrification can create a broader development dividend. Investment in renewable energy, grids, storage and clean technologies can support green jobs, build domestic value chains and drive green industrialization, to power that businesses and communities need to grow.

But realizing this opportunity will require investment in generation and grids, while addressing the upfront costs that can prevent households and businesses from benefiting. Around 1.18 billion people still experience energy poverty, while Africa receives only 2% of global clean energy investment.

UNDP is supporting this effort alongside around 30 UN entities, with the aim of helping at least 100 countries build the policies and project pipelines needed to put finance to work.

The opportunity is not simply to electrify more of the global economy, but to use electrification to build more secure, resilient and inclusive economies. By 2035, can we ensure that growing electricity demand translates into new industries and green jobs, while also delivering reliable and affordable energy to hospitals, businesses and households?
